Question: How can a patient request a copy of their personal data or medical records, what contact details are given, and does the page mention any form or method?
A patient can request a copy of any personal data the hospital holds by making a subject access request (SAR). Requests must be received in writing either by email or post, accompanied by proof of identity, and the SAR form will be emailed upon request. Contact details given are aio@stjames.ie, (01) 410 3010, (01) 416 2485, and the Data Protection Office at dataprotection@stjames.ie, (01) 410 3021; yes, the page mentions forms, including a Subject Access Request (SAR) Form.

Question: What does this page say about requesting records, the format of release, and who to contact?
Requests can be made to the Access to Information Office by writing or by completing and returning one of the listed request forms. step.detail:
Question: What does the Ombudsman say about reviewing complaints about public hospitals? Is there a time limit, and how does someone apply?
The Ombudsman says you must first complain to the HSE or the service provider using its complaints procedure, and then you can complain to the Ombudsman if you are still unhappy. Yes, there is a time limit: you should submit your complaint within 12 months of the action or decision, though they may still help after that if there is a good reason for the delay. You can complain through the Ombudsman website, or by writing to the Office of the Ombudsman in Dublin or calling them.

Question: Who runs the hospital, how can a patient complain, what stages and response times are described, and what time limits or next steps are stated? উদ্ধ quotes needed.
The page says the hospital is St James’s Hospital, and complaints are handled through the Patient Experience Office / Complaints Officer, with options to contact them by telephone, email or letter, or raise the issue with the nurse in charge of a ward or a department manager. It describes these stages: give feedback, leave a comment/feedback (no formal response), make a formal complaint, request an Internal Review if dissatisfied with the hospital’s response, and then seek an independent external review from the Ombudsman. The only time limit stated is that an Internal Review “should be requested within 30 days of receiving the Hospital’s response,” and it also says a formal complaint may be followed by an Ombudsman review if the complaint remains unresolved.

step.detail:
Question: What contributions or free legal aid rules does this page give, and does it mention any cases that are free?
The page says most people seeking civil legal aid must pay a contribution: an advice contribution of at least €30 and up to €150, and if represented in court an aid contribution of at least €130, with the aid amount including the advice contribution. It also says asylum or subsidiary protection legal aid has a €10 contribution, that contributions can be waived for undue hardship, and that some cases are free: barring/safety/interim barring/protection orders and defending Tusla applications to take children into foster care or supervise them at home. It adds that there are "a small number of other circumstances where we will not charge a contribution."

Contributions - Legal Aid Board (https://www.legalaidboard.ie/our-legal-aid-service/apply-now/financial-eligibility-and-merits-test/contributions/)
The page says most people seeking civil legal aid must pay a contribution: an advice contribution of at least €30 and up to €150, and if represented in court an aid contribution of at least €130, with the aid amount including the advice contribution. It also says asylum or subsidiary protection legal aid has a €10 contribution, that contributions can be waived for undue hardship, and that some cases are free: barring/safety/interim barring/protect…

say.detail: The page says most people seeking civil legal aid must pay a contribution: an advice contribution of at least €30 and up to €150, and if represented in court an aid contribution of at least €130, with the aid amount including the advice contribution. It also says asylum or subsidiary protection legal aid has a €10 contribution, that contributions can be waived for undue hardship, and that some cases are free: barring/safety/interim barring/protection orders and defending Tusla applications to take children into foster care or supervise them at home. It adds that there are "a small number of other circumstances where we will not charge a contribution."

Question: What does this page say about how civil cases start and whether a personal injury claim is likely heard by a judge only or before a jury?
Civil cases that are not settled out of court are scheduled for trial before a judge. For personal injury claims, the page says you start your claim through the Injuries Resolution Board, and such cases are most likely heard by a judge only rather than a jury.

step.detail:
Question: What does this page say about how a patient gets compensation for hospital negligence in Ireland, including court or PIAB, time limit, and whether there is any cap or no-fault scheme? Quote the relevant lines and note any links to official sources.
The page says most hospital negligence claims in Ireland are usually brought through the courts, and that most such claims go to the High Court rather than the Circuit Court. It says clinical negligence claims are exempt from the IRB/PIAB mandatory assessment process, so proceedings can be issued directly through the High Court, and it gives a 2-year limitation period from the date of injury or date of knowledge. It also says there is no cap mentioned on compensation here; instead it refers to the Judicial Council Personal Injuries Guidelines, and it does not describe any no-fault compensation scheme for hospital negligence.
✓ quote found in the page: "Almost all hospital negligence claims exceed the €60,000 Circuit Court personal injury threshold, so they're heard in the High Court."

✓ quote found in the page: "The legal principles governing hospital negligence in Ireland are identical whether your care was in a public HSE hospital or a private facility. The same Dunne test applies, the same two-year limitation period runs, and the same Judicial Council Personal Injuries Guidelines (2021) are used to assess compensation."

A patient can request a copy of any personal data the hospital holds by making a subject access request (SAR). Requests must be received in writing either by email or post, accompanied by proof of identity, and the SAR form will be emailed upon request. Contact details given are aio@stjames.ie, (01) 410 3010, (01) 416 2485, and the Data Protection Office at dataprotection@stjames.ie, (01) 410 3021; yes, the page mentions forms, including a Subject Access Request (SAR) Form.

Requests can be made to the Access to Information Office by writing or by completing and returning one of the listed request forms. The request should include a statement that it is made under the FOI Act, as much information as possible about the records sought, and the format in which you want to receive any released records (for example, photocopies). For help, the page says to email aio@stjames.ie or call (01) 410 3010 or (01) 410 3807.

The page says Ireland is developing clinical effectiveness through the National Clinical Effectiveness Committee (NCEC): “Ireland is developing Clinical Effectiveness through the National Clinical Effectiveness Committee (NCEC) that the Minister of Health set up in 2010.”

The page says formal complaints can be sent to the Patient Experience Office / Complaints Officer by phone, email, or in writing. The contact details given are Phone 1: 01 410 3361, Phone 2: 01 428 4248, and patientfeedback@stjames.ie, at St James’s Hospital, James Street, Dublin 8. For hospital operator/ownership wording, the page itself is branded HSE.ie and says the Patient Experience Office works with hospital staff, but it does not give a separate owner/operator description for the hospital.

If you are still not happy with the outcome/decision of the complaints officer, you can request an internal review of your complaint, which is Stage 3. The page says this is reviewed internally, but it does not say by whom, when you can go, by when, or how to apply for it. It only says you can then “move directly to Stage 4 and seek an independent review of your complaint.”

The page says the hospital is St James’s Hospital, and complaints are handled through the Patient Experience Office / Complaints Officer, with options to contact them by telephone, email or letter, or raise the issue with the nurse in charge of a ward or a department manager. It describes these stages: give feedback, leave a comment/feedback (no formal response), make a formal complaint, request an Internal Review if dissatisfied with the hospital’s response, and then seek an independent external review from the Ombudsman. The only time limit stated is that an Internal Review “should be requested within 30 days of receiving the Hospital’s response,” and it also says a formal complaint may be followed by an Ombudsman review if the complaint remains unresolved.

The National Clinical Effectiveness Committee (NCEC) has that role. Exact wording: “The role of the National Clinical Effectiveness Committee (NCEC) is to recommend guidelines and audit to the Minister for Health to become NCEC National Clinical Guidelines and NCEC National Clinical Audit for implementation in Irish healthcare.”

The Ombudsman says you must first complain to the HSE or the service provider using its complaints procedure, and then you can complain to the Ombudsman if you are still unhappy. Yes, there is a time limit: you should submit your complaint within 12 months of the action or decision, though they may still help after that if there is a good reason for the delay. You can complain through the Ombudsman website, or by writing to the Office of the Ombudsman in Dublin or calling them.
